title: Dense pentacene cocrystal demonstrates room-temperature coherent control
authors: Noella D'Souza, Guangzhao Chen, Madhur Parashar, Wern Ng, Brandon Wallace, Tatiana Lindahl, Tanner S. Volek, Lam Lam, Joseph Garrett, Emanuel Druga, Sean T. Roberts, Jeffrey Reimer, Harpreet Singh, Liang Z. Tan, Riccardo Montis, Ashok Ajoy
abstract: Maximizing the number of addressable spins within a fixed volume can improve ensemble quantum sensor sensitivity, but dense packing usually increases dipolar interactions and excited-state transport, shortening coherence and suppressing optical readout. Here we report a 2:1 cocrystal of 6,13-dihydropentacene and pentacene (DHP/Pc) containing 33.3 mol% pentacene ($3.3\times10^{5}$ ppm; $9.51\times10^{20}$ cm$^{-3}$), a volumetric spin-site density more than two orders of magnitude above previous benchmarks, NV-diamond and pentacene-doped p-terphenyl (PDP). Despite this density, DHP/Pc exhibits microsecond spin coherence, room-temperature optically detected magnetic resonance and coherent control. Time-resolved measurements indicate that the long-lived triplet population is generated predominantly by intersystem crossing and exhibits strong, non-thermal sublevel polarization. Density-functional theory calculations further suggest that the native cocrystal geometry weakens electronic coupling between neighboring pentacenes, while the higher DHP triplet energy creates a barrier to triplet migration. These results identify molecular packing and coformer triplet energetics as complementary design parameters for preserving coherence in high spin-site density systems, demonstrating cocrystallization as a promising route to dense, optically addressable spin materials for room-temperature ensemble quantum sensing.
summary: The authors report on a novel pentacene cocrystal that achieves an unprecedentedly high density of addressable spin centers while maintaining long spin coherence times at room temperature. By combining spectroscopic measurements with DFT calculations, they demonstrate that the specific molecular packing and energy offsets within the cocrystal suppress detrimental interactions, making it a promising material for quantum sensing.
main_problem: The central challenge is increasing the spin-site density in quantum materials for sensing while preventing coherence loss due to strong dipolar interactions and excited-state transport.
main_result: The DHP/Pc cocrystal achieves ultra-high spin-site density with preserved microsecond spin coherence and room-temperature coherent control, demonstrating cocrystallization as a viable design strategy.
method: The study combines time-resolved spectroscopy (EPR, absorption) to measure coherence and triplet dynamics with DFT calculations to model electronic coupling and energy barriers.
model_or_system: The physical system is a 2:1 cocrystal of 6,13-dihydropentacene and pentacene (DHP/Pc), which serves as a dense platform for addressable spin centers.
key_observables: Microsecond spin coherence ($T_2$), room-temperature Optically Detected Magnetic Resonance (ODMR) resonances, triplet sublevel polarization ratios ($P_X:P_Y:P_Z$), and electronic coupling strengths.

main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that molecular packing and coformer triplet energetics can be independently tuned to maintain coherence in dense systems.
figures_summary: Figures show SEM/XRD confirming the dense lattice structure, EPR/TAM comparing triplet generation pathways (ISC vs. SF), and ODMR/CPMG sequences demonstrating coherent control and linewidth measurements.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem of density vs. coherence, then uses spectroscopy (EPR/ODMR) to characterize the high-density state, followed by DFT calculations to provide a theoretical underpinning for the observed coherence preservation mechanism.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the fundamental trade-off between material density and quantum coherence, providing concrete structural and energetic design rules (molecular packing and triplet energetics) for realizing practical, high-density quantum sensors.
